title: Chinese Food: Best Food?
summary: Josh and Chuck give a broad overview of Chinese food as it has developed in the United States, covering the eight regional cuisines of China, Cantonese roots and early San Francisco restaurants, chop suey and the Lem Sen lawsuit, how immigration law (Chinese Exclusion Act, merchant status, 1965 Immigration Act) shaped restaurants, the labor system of Chinese restaurants, American dishes like General Tso's chicken, crab rangoon, fortune cookies, broccoli beef, and chow mein sandwiches, the history of PF Chang's and Panda Express, and how Chinese food was adapted in the UK, India, Latin America, and South Africa. The episode closes with a listener mail correction about the Tulipmania myth.

entities.name: From Canton Restaurant to Panda Express

segments.title: Intro and caveats
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode as a broad overview of Chinese food, with caveats about pronunciation and scope, focusing on American Chinese food and personal favorites.

segments.title: Eight regional cuisines of China
segments.summary: Chinese food varies by region and has been adapted abroad. The hosts list China's eight regional cuisines and discuss how coastal, cold, and game-rich regions differ in flavors, including numbing Sichuan peppercorns and chilies.

segments.title: Cantonese cuisine and dim sum
segments.summary: Cantonese cuisine is the style most Americans know, tied to early migrants from Canton. The first Chinese restaurant in North America, Canton, opened in San Francisco in 1849. Dim sum is described as shared small plates.

segments.title: Early Chinese restaurants and anti-Chinese racism
segments.summary: Chinese restaurants in the Gold Rush era hung yellow flags. Racist attitudes toward Chinese immigrants and their food appeared early, including a 1865 court example and a 1902 Samuel Gompers pamphlet. The Pekin Noodle Parlor in Montana is named as the oldest continuously operating Chinese restaurant in the US.

segments.title: Chop suey origins and the Lem Sen lawsuit
segments.summary: Chop suey is described as a mix of meat, vegetables and thick sauce, with debated origins and name meaning. In 1904 Lem Sen sued, claiming he invented chop suey; he later dropped the suit. The hosts tie this to the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 and its quota.

segments.title: Chop suey's spread and American Chinese dishes
segments.summary: Chop suey became an umbrella term for Chinese dishes in America and spread out of Chinatowns. Lachoy canned sauce was sold for decades, and chop suey was included in a 1942 US Army cookbook, with restaurants overseas serving it to American soldiers.

segments.title: Merchant status and the restaurant boom
segments.summary: The Exclusion Act's merchant status clause let restaurant owners sponsor relatives; a 1915 court case added Chinese restaurants to it. This led to upscale chop suey palaces and a boom in restaurants, which was renewed after the 1965 Immigration and Nationality Act.

segments.title: Labor and staffing of Chinese restaurants
segments.summary: Forty thousand Chinese restaurants in the US in 2014 were run by families and staffed by new immigrants, many from Fujian and some undocumented, hired through Chinese-language employment agencies. Cooks move often, and restaurants bought from Cantonese owners keep the same American menus.

segments.title: General Tso's chicken
segments.summary: The hosts discuss General Tso's chicken and its origin with chef Peng Chang-kuei in Taiwan, named after a Qing dynasty general. It was transformed when exported to the US, and delivery data show it as a popular takeout dish.

segments.title: Crab rangoon, cheese, and Americanized ingredients
segments.summary: Crab rangoon, invented by an American, is cream cheese-filled and found in most American Chinese restaurants. The hosts discuss other Americanized ingredients, including beef with broccoli and broccoli's supposed link to Thomas Jefferson.

segments.title: Fortune cookies
segments.summary: Fortune cookies derive from a Japanese cracker, and Chinese Americans later took over cookie factories. Donald Lau, CFO of Wonton Food Company, wrote fortunes for about thirty years.

segments.title: Regional specialties: Saint Paul and Fall River sandwiches
segments.summary: The hosts describe the Saint Paul sandwich, an egg foo young sandwich with brown gravy, and the chow mein sandwich from Fall River, Massachusetts, served on a hamburger bun.

segments.title: Mid-episode break
segments.summary: Hosts announce a break before the PF Chang's and Panda Express segment.

segments.title: PF Chang's and the chain restaurant side
segments.summary: The hosts discuss PF Chang's as a step up from takeout but a chain. They also plug the Factory Seconds podcast about the Cheesecake Factory menu.

segments.title: Cecilia Chiang, Mandarin, and PF Chang's origins
segments.summary: Cecilia Chiang opened the high-end Mandarin restaurant in San Francisco in 1961, avoiding chop suey and egg foo young, and introduced more authentic dishes. Her son Philip Chiang co-founded PF Chang's after buying Mandarin in 1989.

segments.title: Panda Express
segments.summary: Panda Express has about 2,300 US locations, more than PF Chang's. It is a family business that grew from a few sit-down restaurants in the 1970s, and it debuted orange chicken in 1987.

segments.title: Chinese food abroad: UK, India, Latin America
segments.summary: The hosts discuss British Chinese food, including chicken balls and curry sauce, Indian Chinese dishes like Manchurian, and Chinese-Latin American cuisine such as Chino-Latino food in New York and Cuban-Chinese blends.

segments.title: Afro-Cantonese cuisine in South Africa
segments.summary: Afro-Cantonese cuisine in South Africa developed from indentured Chinese workers in the nineteenth century. The hosts express interest in trying it and mention a possible future Cajun food episode.

segments.title: Show anniversary and friend mention
segments.summary: Chuck notes the show's seventeenth anniversary and mentions friend Doug Shasherie, prompting listener mail.

segments.title: Listener correction on Tulipmania
segments.summary: A listener named Richard corrects an earlier short stuff episode, saying the Tulipmania story is now largely believed to be a myth, citing historian Anne Goldgar and Charles Mackay's book. Chuck responds that the sources used were varied and that the claim that it is a myth is contested.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts close the episode and direct listeners to send mail to the show.
